main.t: The single bone of the back and base of the skull, around the foramen magnum (occipital bone).

simpler.t: The occipital bone is the bone at the back of your head.

deeper.t: Its condyles rest on the first cervical vertebra, so the skull sits on the vertebral column.

facts.t: It forms the back of the skull and the back of the base of the cranial cavity.
It meets the two parietal bones and the temporal bones at the lambdoid suture.
Inside, it forms the floor and back wall of the posterior cranial fossa.

simpler.t: It is at the back of your head, down to where your skull sits on your neck.

deeper.t: The posterior cranial fossa is the deepest of the three, and holds the cerebellum.

items.name: External occipital protuberance
items.t: A small bump at the back midline, where a ligament of the neck attaches.

items.name: Superior nuchal lines
items.t: Lines either side of the bump: the highest point where neck muscles attach.

items.name: Foramen magnum
items.t: The large opening (“great aperture”) in the base, for the spinal cord.

items.name: Occipital condyles
items.t: Oval knobs either side of the foramen magnum, which form joints with the first cervical vertebra.

items.name: Hypoglossal canals
items.t: Openings at the front edge of the foramen magnum, for a nerve to the tongue.

items.name: Venous grooves
items.t: Large curved grooves on the inner wall, ending at the jugular foramen.

simpler.t: It has a bump at the back, a large hole underneath and two knobs that sit on the spine.

deeper.t: Above the nuchal lines only the scalp covers the skull; below them, neck muscles attach.

facts.t: Its condyles form joints with the first cervical vertebra, supporting the skull on the spine.
The foramen magnum lets the spinal cord pass out of the skull.
Its protuberance and nuchal lines anchor a ligament and the muscles of the back of the neck.

simpler.t: It holds your head on your neck and lets the spinal cord out.

items.name: First cervical vertebra (atlas)
items.t: Supports the skull: it forms joints with the occipital condyles.

items.name: Spinal cord
items.t: Leaves the skull through the foramen magnum.

items.name: Cerebellum
items.t: Lies in the posterior cranial fossa.

items.name: Vertebral arteries
items.t: Enter the skull through the foramen magnum to supply the brain and spinal cord.

items.name: Hypoglossal nerve
items.t: The motor nerve of the tongue; it passes through the hypoglossal canal.

items.name: Lambdoid suture
items.t: Joins it to the parietal and temporal bones.

simpler.t: It sits on the first neck vertebra and lets the spinal cord and two arteries through.

facts.t: Its upper part, behind the brain, forms from membrane; its base forms from a cartilage model.
facts.check: OpenStax says the top and sides of the brain case form from membrane, and its floor from cartilage; how this divides the occipital bone needs an approved source.

items.injury: A blow to the front or side of the head.
items.damaged: The base of the occipital bone may break on the opposite side (contrecoup), a basilar fracture.
items.cannotDo: Rely on the site of the blow to show where the skull broke.
items.why: In a contrecoup fracture, the bone breaks opposite the point of impact.

items.injury: Bleeding or swelling raises the pressure inside the skull.
items.damaged: The lowest part of the cerebellum is pushed down through the foramen magnum.
items.cannotDo: Keep breathing and heart rate regulated: the brainstem is compressed.
items.why: The pons and medulla, at the foramen magnum, regulate breathing and the heart.
items.check: Herniation through the foramen magnum is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20); the brainstem’s role is.

items.q: Explain how the skull is supported on the vertebral column.
model: The occipital bone has an oval condyle on each side of the foramen magnum.
The condyles form joints with the first cervical vertebra.
This vertebra is called the atlas because it supports the skull.
So the skull rests on top of the vertebral column.

items.q: Compare the foramen magnum and the hypoglossal canal.
model: The foramen magnum is the large opening in the base of the occipital bone.
It carries the spinal cord and the vertebral arteries.
The hypoglossal canal is a small opening at its front edge.
It carries the hypoglossal nerve, the motor nerve of the tongue.

items.q: Predict why a blow to the forehead can break the occipital bone.
model: The bone at the point of impact does not break.
Instead, the skull breaks on the opposite side.
At the base of the skull this gives a basilar fracture.

check.stem: What passes through the foramen magnum?
check.why: The foramen magnum allows passage of the spinal cord as it exits the skull.

check.stem: Which bone do the occipital condyles meet?
check.why: They form joints with the first cervical vertebra, the atlas.

check.stem: Which part of the brain lies in the posterior cranial fossa?
check.why: The posterior cranial fossa contains the cerebellum.
